thread.title: Fund Managers' Latest Worry: Corporate Debt

author: Barron's
title: Fund Managers' Latest Worry: Corporate Debt
text:
Photograph by Rolf Vennenbernd/AFP/Getty Images Fund managers are becoming more concerned about corporate debt, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch's latest monthly survey.
For the first time since 2009, debt reduction has risen above capital spending on fund managers' list of priorities for companies, according to the bank.
This shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone who paid attention to markets in November, when shares of blue-chip companies like General Electric (ticker: GE) and AT&T ( T ) sank on concern about their debt levels. The survey's results show just how widespread the concerns about corporate debt have become.
Nearly half of the 190 respondents (who manage $575 billion) said that companies' cash hoard should be used to reduce debt levels before anything else. That 46% share was the highest since 2009, according to the bank.
Capital expenditures were the top priority for 34% of the fund managers surveyed. Only 13% said that shareholder returns should be companies' top priority.
Read more: Rising Interest Rates Complicate the Corporate Borrowing Spree
Of course, investors don't always back their survey responses with their cash. Companies have recently been rewarded by shareholders for taking on more debt, as we reported last week.
Another reason for fund managers' concerns about credit could be their increasingly dim outlook for global economic growth.
More than half (53%) of fund managers said that global growth will weaken over the next year, the highest share since October 2008.
But they think the U.S. will fare better than the rest of the world, going by the survey results. The most "crowded trade" is the bet on a stronger dollar, according to Merrill.
https://asset.barrons.com/dj-mg/dice/barrons-staffpicks-2d590600-c862-4394-b9d3-66b48c376d60/inset.json
Before December, the strong-dollar trade was less crowded than bullish bets on the big tech companies known as "FAANG+BAT": Facebook ( FB ), Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), Netflix ( NFLX ) and Alphabet (GOOGL), plus Baidu (BIDU), Alibaba Group Holding (BABA), and Tencent Holdings (0700.Hong Kong) in Asia.
That might have something to do with the prospect of a trade war, which fund managers named as the biggest "tail risk" they see.
Of course, when these tail-risk worries show up on polls, it is often a sign that they are already priced in to markets.
But December was the seventh consecutive month that a trade war topped the list-so this fear might linger a bit longer than most.
